docs.title: Safety
docs.text: STEPFOC is a bare circuit board that drives a motor from a supply of up to 29 V. Read this chapter before you connect anything; the few rules here are the ones that destroy a driver, a motor or a finger when they are ignored.

docs.title: Electrical
docs.text:
Supply polarity

Reversing the polarity on DC+ and DC− destroys the driver at once. Check the polarity of every power cable before you plug it in, every time.

Cable orientation on the daisy chain

The CAN and power cables that link one driver to the next are keyed by their orientation, not by their connector: a cable plugged in the wrong way round puts the supply on the wrong pins and destroys the driver. Use the cables from the Source Robotics shop, or make yours exactly as shown in Power and the CAN daisy chain.

UART is 3.3 V

The UART port runs at 3.3 V. A 5 V serial adapter destroys the board. Use a 3.3 V adapter, such as the one from the shop.

Supply voltage

12 to 29 V DC. The driver raises a Vbus error outside 9 to 29.5 V, but the hardware limit is 29 V: do not connect a supply that can rise above it, and allow for the voltage a decelerating motor pushes back into the supply. A bench supply with a current limit is the safest way to start.

Do not disconnect a running motor

Never unplug a motor, or a power cable in the daisy chain, while the driver is powered. The inductive kick of the coils and the arcing at the connector damage the driver stage.

docs.title: Mechanical
docs.text:
Moving parts

A calibrating or running motor turns without warning, in both directions, and the stepper in position mode pushes back hard against a hand. Keep fingers, hair and cables away from the shaft and whatever is mounted on it, fix the motor to the bench before the first test, and test without a load on the shaft.

The encoder magnet

The magnet sits about 1 mm above the encoder chip. A magnet that touches the chip, or sits far too close, can damage the microcontroller; a magnet too far away gives a wrong position. Mount it as described in The encoder magnet.

Hot motor and driver

A stepper running at its rated current gets hot enough to burn. Set the current limit for your motor (Current limit and loop tuning), use the thermistor, and give the driver airflow when it runs near 2.8 A.

docs.title: Stopping the motor
docs.text:
• Send_ESTOP over CAN, or #Idle over UART, stops the motor at once; the E-stop error stays until it is cleared.
  • Cutting the supply stops the motor as well; a stepper then holds nothing, so a vertical axis drops.
  • The watchdog (Send_Watchdog) stops the motor by itself when the host stops talking.

Nothing on the driver is a certified safety function. A machine that can hurt someone needs an emergency stop that cuts the motor supply, independent of the driver.

docs.title: Firmware updates and programming
docs.text: When you connect a programming adapter to the JTAG connector, disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter first. Updating over the bootloader needs no adapter; see Firmware.

docs.text: STEPFOC is sold as a component for people who build their own machines. docs.title: Low-quality motors
docs.text: Motors with visibly bad windings, an uneven back-EMF or a resistance that differs between the two coils calibrate poorly and run rough. The tested motors are known good.

docs.title: The magnet and the encoder
docs.text:
• The distance is 1 mm. "Magnet Good" from the magnet test does not mean the distance is right, only that the field is strong enough.
  • A magnet touching the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet too far gives a noisy, wrong position.
  • The magnet must be diametrically magnetised and centred on the shaft.

docs.title: The driver gets hot or shuts down
docs.text: The MOSFET driver stage shuts down on its own overtemperature or overcurrent and reports a driver error. Lower the current limit, give the board airflow, check the motor leads for a short. Near 2.8 A the driver needs cooling.

docs.title: After a firmware update
docs.text: #Info shows the new release. If the values look wrong or the LED stays on: #Default, enter the motor parameters, #Cal, #Save. A release note says when an update clears the calibration.

docs.title: Scope and audience
docs.text:
The STEPFOC Manual covers the STEPFOC stepper driver from unpacking to a tuned motor on a CAN bus: what the driver is, how to mount it on a motor and wire it, the first setup over the serial terminal, calibration and tuning, how the driver is controlled over UART and CAN or from Python, and how its firmware is updated. The Reference lists every CAN message and UART command of the firmware release named on the landing page. The Guides are worked examples.

It is written for someone who builds a robot or a machine with STEPFOC: a maker, a student or an engineer who can solder four motor wires and open a serial terminal. It does not assume any knowledge of field-oriented control; the Theory corner in the appendix explains the concepts the control modes rely on.

Read the Safety chapter before you power anything. The Quick start is the whole first setup on one page; the chapters are in the order you need them and go deeper.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
The header has four tabs. STEPFOC Manual is the document you read from the start: the quick start, then safety, technical data, mounting, the first setup, operation and firmware updates, in numbered chapters. Motor GUI, the tool in the browser, is the usual way to do what the chapters describe; each procedure shows it first and the terminal command beside it. API reference lists every CAN message, every UART command and the Python library's calls for the firmware release this site describes, with the defaults and the error flags, and is where you look things up. Guides are worked examples with code. Support says where to get help and how to report a problem.

The whole site describes one firmware release. The dropdown next to the site name switches between releases, and a page from an older release says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the firmware repository; every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report a problem with it.

docs.title: Warnings and notes
docs.text:
Three kinds of highlighted text appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on the step it belongs to.

Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

Notice

The robot, the tool, or data on the control box can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

Danger

Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
From the box to a calibrated motor that follows commands, on one page. The quickest way through is Motor GUI in the browser; every step also shows the terminal commands, and ends with a link to the chapter that explains it. Follow the link when a step is not clear or something fails.

Read first

Reversed supply polarity, a daisy-chain cable the wrong way round, or 5 V on the UART port destroys the driver. The motor turns during calibration. The Safety chapter is two minutes long.

docs.title: 1. What you need
docs.text:
Where to get it STEPFOC driver single driver or the starter kit, which has everything below except the motor and the supply A bipolar stepper motor with a rear shaft: NEMA 17, 1 to 5 Ω per coil, 3 A or less the tested motors are safe choices The encoder magnet, diametrically magnetised; the stock one is 6 × 2.5 mm, another thickness is fine if it gives the 1 mm gap magnet A spacer for your motor length and four longer M3 screws printable spacers in Stepper motor accessories USB-to-serial adapter, 3.3 V, and its cable serial adapter, UART cable Power cable power cable A 12 to 29 V supply, 24 V recommended a bench supply with a current limit is the safest start For CAN later: CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter and a CAN cable CAN adapter, CAN cable Optional: 100 kΩ NTC thermistor for motor temperature protection thermistor Software: Motor GUI in Chrome or Edge, or a serial terminal motorgui.com; PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino serial monitor

Read in more detail: What you need.

docs.title: 2. Fit the magnet
docs.text:
Press the magnet onto the rear shaft, centred, and glue it. It must end up about 1 mm above the encoder chip in the middle of the board, and it must not be able to turn on the shaft. A magnet that slips is the usual cause of a calibration that "succeeds" and a motor that then runs badly.

Read in more detail: The encoder magnet.

docs.title: 3. Mount the board
docs.text:
Remove the motor's four rear screws, put the spacer on, the board on the spacer with the encoder chip towards the magnet, and the longer screws in. Check the gap: 1 mm, not touching.

Read in more detail: Mounting on the motor.

docs.title: 4. Wire the motor
docs.text:
Find the two coils with a multimeter (the two wires of a coil show a few ohms; wires of different coils show nothing). Solder one coil to A+ and A−, the other to B+ and B−. Which coil is which, and which way round, does not matter: calibration detects it.

Read in more detail: Wiring the stepper.

docs.title: 5. Connect power and the PC
docs.text:
1. The supply to a power connector: DC+ to positive, DC− to negative. Check twice.
  2. The serial adapter to the UART connector with the UART cable (TX to RX, RX to TX; 3.3 V only).
  3. Power on. The LED turns on steadily: the driver is not calibrated yet, which it reports as an error state.
Motor GUITerminal

Open motorgui.com in Chrome or Edge, choose the serial connection and Open port on the adapter's port. The driver's identity and state appear: hardware and firmware version, serial number, Not calibrated, No errors. If nothing connects: the port, the cable's TX/RX, the browser (Web Serial needs a Chromium browser).

Read in more detail: Motor GUI.

Open a terminal on the adapter's port, 256000 baud, line ending CR+LF, and type #Info. The driver prints its hardware and firmware version and the state of everything.

Read in more detail: The serial terminal.

Read in more detail: Power and the CAN daisy chain · Connectors and pinout.

docs.title: 6. Enter the motor parameters
docs.text:
From the motor's datasheet, for one coil: the pole pairs (50 for a 1.8° motor, 100 for 0.9°), the phase resistance in ohms, the phase inductance in henries (2.6 mH = 0.0026). STEPFOC does not measure these; calibration fails on a value left at 0.

Motor GUITerminal

Enter Pole pairs, Resistance and Inductance in the motor settings and apply them.

#PP 50
#R 1.1
#L 0.0026

Read in more detail: Motor parameters and calibration.

docs.title: 7. Calibrate
docs.text:
Fix the motor to the bench, nothing on the shaft, 24 V on the supply.

Motor GUITerminal

Start the calibration. The GUI switches to Calibration mode and shows the driver's log step by step.

#Cal

The LED flashes, the motor turns in both directions, and the driver reports each step: the pole pairs, the magnet, the supply, the parameters you entered, the open-loop spin, the angle offset, the motor constants, and finally

Calibration success!
Save config with #Save
Going to idle!

A failed step names itself. Magnet test: Failed is the magnet; Open loop: Failed or Phase order is wrong! means the motor did not turn or did not respond: check the four wires, the supply, and that the magnet does not slip.

Read in more detail: Motor parameters and calibration, with the whole log and every message.

docs.title: 8. Set the current limit and save
docs.text:
The current limit is the motor's rated phase current in mA; the firmware's default is higher than a small motor's rating.

Motor GUITerminal

Set the current limit in the limits, then Save (the GUI warns about unsaved changes until you do).

#Ilim 1500
#Save

Without saving, the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. The LED now shows three short flashes and a pause: normal operation.

Read in more detail: Current limit and loop tuning · Saving the configuration.

docs.title: 9. Move it
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Use the jog controls: Jog velocity turns the motor at a speed, Jog position moves it to a position, Jog current applies a torque; Send setpoint sends a value in the current control mode. The plots show position, speed and current while it moves.

#V 16384        one revolution per second
#V 0
#P 0            back to where it started
#P 16384        one revolution forward
#Idle

Position is in encoder ticks, 16384 per revolution; speed in ticks per second; current in mA. If the motor hums or whines, lower the current limit or tune the loops.

Read in more detail: Control modes · Current limit and loop tuning.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Activated A flag the driver keeps (#Activate, Send_gripper_data_pack). In gripper mode a move is carried out only while the gripper is activated. ADDITIONAL2 A spare pin of the driver, usable as an analog input or a digital input/output. HALL mode homes the motor against a sensor wired to it. Angle offset (theta offset) The angle between the encoder's zero and the motor's electrical zero, found by calibration and stored. The driver needs it to place the current vector relative to the rotor. Back-EMF The voltage a turning motor generates in its own coils, proportional to speed. It opposes the supply, limits the top speed at a given voltage, and is what calibration measures to find KV, Kt and the flux linkage. Board ID The bootloader's own address, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. The firmware keeps it equal to the CAN node ID. Bootloader The program in the first 12 KB of the driver's flash on boards shipped with firmware 104 or newer. It starts the firmware, and loads a new firmware over UART or CAN. See The bootloader. Calibration The routine (#Cal) that checks the magnet and the supply, takes the motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs, computes the current loop gains, spins the motor in open loop to learn the wiring, finds the angle offset and measures Kt, KV and the flux linkage. Its result is kept with #Save. CAN ID (node ID) The address of the driver on the CAN bus, 0 to 15. It occupies bits 10 to 7 of the 11-bit CAN frame identifier; the command ID occupies bits 6 to 1 and the error bit is bit 0. CANvas Source Robotics' USB-to-CAN adapter. It appears as a serial port and speaks slcan, which python-can and Motor GUI use. Command ID The number, 0 to 63, in bits 6 to 1 of a CAN frame identifier that says which message the frame carries. The API reference lists every command ID. Commutation Placing the stator current so that it produces torque at the rotor's present angle. FOC does it continuously from the encoder angle and the angle offset; a conventional stepper driver does it blindly, step by step. Control mode What the driver is doing with the motor: idle, position, velocity, current, PD (impedance), voltage torque, open loop, HALL, gripper, or calibration. A command that carries a setpoint puts the driver in the matching mode. Current loop bandwidth (#Cbw) How fast the current loop follows a change of its setpoint, in Hz. Calibration computes the current loop gains from it and the motor's resistance and inductance; 500 Hz by default. Daisy chain Several drivers on one CAN bus and one supply, each driver's second CAN and power connector feeding the next. d-q frame The rotating frame of reference FOC works in: the q axis is at right angles to the rotor field and the current on it (Iq) produces torque; the d axis is along the field and its current (Id) produces none, so it is held at 0. Diametrical magnet A disc magnet whose poles are across its diameter, so the field turns with the shaft. The encoder needs this kind; an axially magnetised disc looks the same and does not work. EEPROM The non-volatile memory on the driver that holds the configuration and the calibration. #Save writes it, #Default restores the factory values. Encoder ticks The unit of position: the 14-bit magnetic encoder gives 16384 ticks per revolution of the motor shaft, counted over as many revolutions as the motor makes. Speed is in ticks per second. Error bit Bit 0 of every CAN frame identifier the driver sends: 1 while any error is active. Feedforward A term added to a loop's output from what is known in advance rather than from the error: the motion frames carry a speed and a current feedforward so a host that knows the trajectory can command it directly, leaving the loops to correct the rest. Field-oriented control (FOC) Controlling a motor by regulating the stator current as a vector in the rotor's frame, from a measurement of the rotor angle. On a stepper it replaces the fixed step currents with sinusoidal currents that follow the rotor, which gives smooth, quiet, efficient motion with no lost steps and a known position. Firmware release One build of the firmware, numbered 103, 104, 105, … and tagged V103, V104, … in the firmware repository. #Info prints the release a driver runs. This documentation describes one release; the version selector switches between them. Flux linkage The rotor's magnetic flux as seen by a coil, in weber; found by calibration from the back-EMF, together with KV and Kt. Gripper mode The driver running a gripper (#Gripper 1): jaw positions from 0 (open) to 255 (closed), a speed, a current limit that becomes the grip force, and object detection. HALL mode Homing against a sensor on ADDITIONAL2: the motor turns at a set speed until the sensor triggers, then holds the position reached. Heartbeat A frame (Respond_Heartbeat) the driver sends at a set interval so the host knows it is alive. Off by default. Iq, Id The two components of the motor current in the d-q frame: Iq produces torque, Id is normally held at 0. The current mode's setpoint and limit are Iq values. Impedance (PD) mode The control mode in which the driver behaves like a spring and a damper around a position setpoint, with the stiffness KP and the damping KD, plus a current feedforward. Kt, KV The motor's torque constant (torque per ampere) and velocity constant (speed per volt), found by calibration. Kt turns a current into an estimated torque; KV gives the top speed at a supply voltage. Microstepping Driving a stepper with intermediate current levels between full steps. Only the open-loop commands (#gosteps, #microstep) use it; under FOC the current follows the rotor continuously. Motor GUI Source Robotics' browser tool for the driver: tuning, plots and firmware updates over a serial or CAN adapter. Open loop Driving the motor as a plain stepper, without the encoder in the loop: #Openloop, #gosteps, and the open-loop spin of the calibration. Phase order How the stepper's two coils are connected to A+/A− and B+/B−. Firmware 105 and newer learns the wiring during calibration and compensates it; firmware 103 asks for the wires to be swapped when it is reversed. Pole pairs The number of electrical cycles per mechanical revolution: 50 for a 1.8° stepper, 100 for a 0.9° stepper. Set with #PP before calibration. Remote frame A CAN frame with the RTR bit set and no data: a request. The host asks for data with a remote frame under a command ID, and the driver answers with a data frame under the same ID. Spectral Micro Source Robotics' BLDC driver, on which STEPFOC is built: the same board, firmware and commands, for three-phase brushless motors. Step angle The angle of one full step of a stepper: 1.8° for the common 200-step motor, 0.9° for a 400-step motor. It sets the pole pairs: 360 ÷ (4 × step angle). Termination The 120 Ω resistor the first and the last node of a CAN bus need. The switch on the driver turns it on. Vbus The supply voltage at the driver, measured and printed in mV. Outside the limits the driver raises a Vbus error. Watchdog A timer the driver resets with every valid CAN frame it receives. When it is set (Send_Watchdog) and runs out, the driver reports a watchdog error and stops.

docs.title: The driver at a glance
docs.text:
STEPFOC is a field-oriented controller for bipolar stepper motors. It sits on the back of a NEMA 17 motor, reads the rotor position from a magnet on the motor shaft, and drives the two coils with sinusoidal currents the way a servo drive does, instead of the fixed step currents of a conventional stepper driver. The result is a stepper that runs quietly and efficiently, never loses steps, reports its position, and can be commanded in position, speed, current (torque) or impedance.

Figure 1: The STEPFOC driver, 39 × 39 mm, with the encoder chip in the middle of the board.

docs.title: What is on the board
docs.text:
Part What it does STM32F103CB microcontroller runs the control loops at 6250 Hz and the CAN and UART interfaces 14-bit magnetic encoder (MT6816) reads the position of the magnet on the motor shaft: 16384 ticks per revolution H-bridge driver with inline current sensing drives the two coils with up to 2.8 A and measures the phase currents 16 Kbit EEPROM keeps the configuration and the calibration over a power cycle Two CAN connectors and two power connectors daisy-chain several drivers on one bus and one supply CAN termination switch the 120 Ω resistor the first and the last node need UART connector (3.3 V) the serial terminal: every setting, calibration, tuning Thermistor connector an NTC on the motor for temperature protection ADDITIONAL2 pin an input or output you can use: HALL mode homes against a sensor wired here JTAG connector (1.27 mm) the programming adapter, for installing the bootloader or for development Status LED normal operation, calibration or error, see below

The connectors and their pinout are in Connectors and pinout.

docs.title: What the firmware does
docs.text:
The firmware closes three nested loops on the motor: a current (torque) loop, a velocity loop around it and a position loop around that, plus an impedance (PD) loop that makes the motor behave like a spring and damper. A command picks the loop: a current setpoint, a speed, a position or a PD setpoint. Open-loop stepping, a voltage-torque mode and a homing mode against a sensor exist beside them; Control modes describes each.

The driver protects itself and the motor: it stops on a supply voltage outside the limits, on an encoder fault, on an over-speed, on a motor over-temperature (with the thermistor), on a hardware fault of the driver stage, on an E-stop command and on a watchdog that runs out. The status LED and #Error tell which; see Errors and recovery.

docs.title: How it is controlled
docs.text:
• UART, a 3.3 V serial port at 256000 baud: human-readable commands such as #P 16384, and the only way to run the calibration. See Over UART.
  • CAN, 1 Mbit/s, up to 16 drivers on one bus: compact frames for real-time control from a PC with the CANvas adapter, a microcontroller or a robot control box. See Over CAN.
  • Python, the Spectral-BLDC library on top of CAN. See With Python.
  • Motor GUI, in the browser, over serial or CAN: the usual tool for setup, testing and tuning. See Motor GUI.

docs.title: The status LED
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning three short flashes and a pause normal operation: no error, calibrated flashing every 0.5 s the calibration routine is running on, not flashing error mode: at least one error is active, or the motor is not calibrated

The LED can be turned off with #LED 0.

docs.title: STEPFOC and Spectral Micro
docs.text:
STEPFOC is built on the same board and the same firmware as the Spectral Micro BLDC driver. The Spectral Micro drives three-phase brushless motors; STEPFOC drives two-phase stepper motors. Everything else is shared: the microcontroller, the encoder, the connectors, the CAN and UART interfaces, the Python library, Motor GUI and the bootloader.

What this means in practice:

  • The commands are the same. Every CAN message and UART command in the Reference exists on both drivers, with the same IDs, names and layouts. A program written for one runs on the other.
  • The firmware releases go in step. A STEPFOC release has a Spectral Micro counterpart with the same changes; the compatibility table lists the pairs. The numbers differ by one (STEPFOC 108 is Spectral Micro 107).
  • Calibration differs. A BLDC driver measures the motor's resistance and inductance and finds its pole pairs; STEPFOC cannot, so you enter the three values from the motor's datasheet before calibrating. See Motor parameters and calibration.
  • The motor terminals differ. A+, A−, B+, B− for the two stepper coils instead of U, V, W.
  • Some images on this site show a Spectral Micro. Where a photo or a screenshot shows the BLDC board, the procedure is the same for STEPFOC.

The guides under the Guides tab were written with the Spectral Micro; the code in them runs unchanged on STEPFOC.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: This page lists what a STEPFOC setup is made of, what comes with the driver, and what you buy or make yourself.

docs.title: The driver
docs.text:
STEPFOC is sold as a single driver or as a starter kit in the Source Robotics shop:

  • STEPFOC stepper driver
  • STEPFOC starter kit, which adds the adapters, the magnet, the cables and a thermistor listed below

Every driver is end-of-line tested and ships with the current firmware release and the bootloader already installed, so a driver works out of the box with a serial terminal, the Python library or Motor GUI. The firmware can be updated later without a programming adapter; see Firmware.

docs.title: A stepper motor
docs.text: STEPFOC drives bipolar (4-wire) stepper motors. It is made for the NEMA 17 frame, whose mounting holes match the board, and it also works with NEMA 14 and NEMA 23 motors on an adapter. Look for a motor with a phase resistance of 1 to 5 Ω and a rated current of 3 A or less; the tested motors are known to work.

docs.title: The encoder magnet
docs.text: A diametrically magnetised 6 × 2.5 mm neodymium magnet on the rear of the motor shaft, about 1 mm above the encoder chip in the middle of the board: 6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet. An axially magnetised magnet, or one that wobbles, makes calibration fail or report bad positions. The 6 × 2.5 mm size is the stock one, not a requirement: another thickness is a way to set the 1 mm gap when a shaft or a spacer leaves the wrong distance. The encoder magnet says how to fit it.

docs.title: Adapters and cables
docs.text:
Part Needed for Shop USB-to-serial adapter (3.3 V) the serial terminal: calibration, tuning, any # command Serial adapter CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter CAN control from a PC, the Python library, Motor GUI over CAN CAN adapter CAN cable and power cable daisy-chaining several drivers CAN cable, power cable 100 kΩ NTC thermistor motor temperature protection (optional but recommended) Thermistor JTAG programming adapter only for installing the bootloader on an older board, or for firmware development Programming adapter

Cable orientation

The daisy-chain cables for CAN and power are keyed by their orientation, not by their connector. A cable plugged in the wrong way round destroys the driver. Use the cables from the shop or follow Power and the CAN daisy chain exactly when you make your own.

docs.title: A power supply
docs.text: 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended; see Ratings and limits. Calibrate at 24 V: the motor constants come out wrong at a lower voltage. A bench supply with a current limit is the safest way to start.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
• Motor GUI, in the browser, over the serial adapter or the CAN adapter: the usual tool for setup, calibration, tuning, plots and firmware updates; see Motor GUI.
  • Or a serial terminal: PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor in VS Code, or the Arduino serial monitor; see The serial terminal.
  • The Python library Spectral-BLDC for CAN control from your own programs; see With Python.

docs.text: The numbers: ratings and limits, the connectors with their pinout, the dimensions, and the motors that have been tested with the driver.

docs.text:
Figure 2: The connectors. The motor coils go to A+, A−, B+, B−; the supply to DC+ and DC−. Connector Pins Type Cable Motor A+, A−, B+, B− solder pads the motor's own leads, see Wiring the stepper Power, two of them DC+, DC− JST XH, 2 pins Power cable; the second connector feeds the next driver CAN, two of them CAN H, CAN L JST ZH, 2 pins CAN cable; the second connector feeds the next driver UART 3.3 V, TX, RX, GND JST SH, 4 pins UART cable Thermistor NTC, NTC JST SH, 2 pins the 100 kΩ NTC from the shop or any 100 kΩ NTC JTAG 3.3 V, GND, SWDIO, SWCLK 1.27 mm header Programming adapter ADDITIONAL2 signal, GND pads your sensor; the HALL homing mode reads this pin STEP / DIR STEP, DIR, GND, 24 V header hardware only: the firmware does not support a step/dir interface

Polarity and orientation

DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative; a cable the wrong way round destroys the driver. The daisy-chain cables have an orientation too: see Power and the CAN daisy chain.

Note

  • UART is TX to RX and RX to TX between the driver and the adapter.
  • The UART port and the ADDITIONAL2 pin are 3.3 V. 5 V on either destroys the board.
  • The thermistor pin has a 54.9 kΩ pull-down; the firmware's temperature table is for a 100 kΩ NTC.
  • The CAN termination switch is next to the CAN connectors; ON connects the 120 Ω resistor.

docs.title: Dimensions and CAD
docs.text:
The board is 39 × 39 mm with the four mounting holes on the NEMA 17 pattern (31 mm apart), so it bolts to the back of a NEMA 17 motor with the motor's own screws and a spacer. The encoder chip is exactly in the middle of the board, on the motor shaft's axis.

Figure 3: Board dimensions and hole pattern. The drawing is of the Spectral Micro, which has the same board. Figure 4: The STEP model.

The STEP files of the board, the magnet spacers for different motor lengths and the tool for pressing the magnet onto the shaft are in the firmware repository:

  • STEP files of the board
  • Stepper motor accessories: magnet spacers, NEMA 17 spacers for different motor lengths, NEMA 23 spacers
  • Tools: the magnet tool

CAD and downloads lists everything that can be downloaded.

docs.title: Tested motors
docs.text:
STEPFOC works with bipolar (4-wire) stepper motors whose phase resistance is 1 to 5 Ω and whose rated current is 3 A or less. The motors below have been run on it; the resistance and inductance are the datasheet values of one coil, which is what you enter with #R and #L before calibration.

Motor Frame Pole pairs Phase resistance Phase inductance Rated current Mass 17HS08-1004S NEMA 17, 20 mm 50 3.7 Ω 4.5 mH 1.0 A 140 g Stepperonline 17HS16-2004S1 NEMA 17, 40 mm 50 1.1 Ω 2.6 mH 2.0 A 310 g Stepperonline 17HS24-2104S NEMA 17, 60 mm 50 1.6 Ω 3.0 mH 2.1 A 500 g Stepperonline 23HM22-2804S NEMA 23, 56 mm, 0.9° 100 1.16 Ω 4.2 mH 2.8 A 700 g Stepperonline

Before the first test, set the current limit to the motor's rated current with #Ilim; the firmware's default is higher than the 17HS08's rating. See Current limit and loop tuning.

Choosing a motor

A lower phase resistance and inductance give a higher speed at a given supply voltage; the velocity constant KV that calibration finds tells how fast the motor can turn: roughly 0.8 × Vbus × KV revolutions per minute. Motors with visibly uneven windings or a resistance that differs between the two coils calibrate badly.

docs.title: Mounting and wiring
docs.text:
How the driver goes onto the motor and what gets connected to it: the encoder magnet on the shaft, the board on the motor's back, the two coils to the motor terminals, the supply and the CAN bus, and the thermistor. Do the pages in order; the magnet first, because it is the one thing you cannot check from the outside later.

Figure 5: The motor hardware setup video shows the whole procedure on a NEMA 17 motor.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• The encoder magnet
  • Mounting on the motor
  • Wiring the stepper
  • Power and the CAN daisy chain
  • Thermistor

When all of it is done, continue with First setup.

docs.title: The encoder magnet
docs.text:
The encoder reads a diametrically magnetised magnet on the rear end of the motor shaft. The magnet must sit centred on the shaft's axis, parallel to the board, about 1 mm above the encoder chip, and it must not move. Every calibration problem that is not a wiring problem comes from this magnet.

Figure 6: About 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip in the middle of the board.

docs.title: The magnet
docs.text:
A neodymium disc, diametrically magnetised (north and south across the diameter, not through the thickness). The shop's 6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet is the size the printed spacers are made for. An axially magnetised magnet looks the same and does not work: the magnet test may even pass, and the position is wrong.

The size is not fixed

6 × 2.5 mm is the stock size, not a requirement. Any diametrically magnetised disc of about 6 mm diameter works, and the thickness is a way to set the gap: a thicker magnet brings its face closer to the encoder, a thinner one farther, so with a shaft or a spacer that leaves the wrong distance you can pick the thickness that gives 1 mm instead of changing the spacer. What matters is the 1 mm from the magnet's face to the chip, the magnet centred on the shaft, and the diametrical magnetisation.

docs.title: Fitting it
docs.text:
1. The motor needs a rear shaft. Most NEMA 17 motors have one; a motor without it needs a magnet holder on the front shaft and a different mechanical layout.
  2. Press the magnet onto the shaft centred. The magnet tool in the firmware repository is a printed jig that centres it; a 3D-printed magnet spacer from Stepper motor accessories fits between the shaft and the magnet when the shaft is too short.
  3. Fix it with a drop of glue. A magnet that can turn on the shaft is the classic cause of a calibration that reports success and a motor that then runs badly: the magnet slipped between calibration and use.
  4. Check the height after the board is mounted: with the spacer for your motor length, the gap is 1 mm. A magnet that touches the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet 2 mm away or more gives a weak signal.

docs.title: Checking it
docs.text: With the driver powered and the serial terminal open, #Magnet answers Magnet Good when the chip sees enough field, Magnet Bad when it does not. The calibration routine runs the same test first. "Good" means the field is strong enough; it does not prove the magnet is centred or that it cannot slip.

docs.title: Mounting on the motor
docs.text:
The board has the NEMA 17 hole pattern (31 mm), so it mounts on the back of the motor with the motor's own four rear screws, with a spacer between the motor and the board that sets the magnet height.

  1. Remove the four rear screws of the motor. They hold the motor's end cap; it does not come apart when you remove them one at a time and put the spacer and the board on at once.
  2. Put the spacer on the motor. The firmware repository has printable spacers for common motor lengths in Stepper motor accessories (NEMA 17, a 21.5 mm NEMA 17 version, NEMA 23); for another motor, make a spacer that puts the board 1 mm above the magnet.
  3. Put the board on the spacer, encoder chip towards the magnet, and fit longer screws of the same thread (M3 on a NEMA 17). Tighten them evenly; the board must be parallel to the magnet.
  4. Check the gap: about 1 mm, the magnet not touching the chip.

A NEMA 14 or NEMA 23 motor needs an adapter plate between the motor and the board; the NEMA 23 spacer is in the same folder.

The board is bare

Nothing on the back of the board may touch the motor's housing. Make sure the spacer keeps the board clear of the end cap, and keep metal swarf and screws away from the board while you work.

docs.title: Power and the CAN daisy chain
docs.text:
Each driver has two power connectors (JST XH) and two CAN connectors (JST ZH). The second connector of each pair feeds the next driver, so a chain of drivers hangs on one supply cable and one CAN cable.

Figure 8: Power and CAN pass from driver to driver. The first and the last node on the bus have their termination switch on.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
• 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended. DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative; reversed polarity destroys the driver.
  • The power connectors are rated for 4 A. A chain of drivers shares that: with motors at 1.5 A each, plan for at most two or three drivers per chain that draw their full current at the same time, and feed a longer chain from both ends or from several supplies.
  • A motor that decelerates pushes energy back into the supply. A lab supply or a battery absorbs it; a supply that cannot (some switch-mode supplies) sees its voltage rise, and the driver raises a Vbus error above 29.5 V.

docs.title: The cable orientation
docs.text:
Danger

The daisy-chain cables are keyed by their orientation, not by the connector: the same 2-pin cable fits both ways, and the wrong way puts DC+ on DC−. Every cable must run as in the picture below, the same way at both ends. A wrong cable destroys the driver at the moment it is powered.

Figure 9: The orientation of the daisy-chain cables for CAN and power.

The cables from the shop are made this way: CAN cable, power cable, and all of them under connectors and cables.

docs.title: CAN
docs.text:
• CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. Up to 16 drivers on one bus, each with its own node ID (0 by default; set it with #CANID or Send_CAN_ID and save).
  • Twisted-pair wire; keep the bus short at 1 Mbit/s (a few metres at most).
  • Termination: the first and the last node on the bus need a 120 Ω resistor between CAN H and CAN L. The switch next to the CAN connectors turns the driver's resistor on (ON). Drivers in the middle stay off. A bus with the right termination measures about 60 Ω between CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered.
  • A PC joins the bus with the CANvas adapter, which has its own termination.
Figure 10: The termination switch, ON for the first and the last node.

docs.title: Thermistor
docs.text:
A 100 kΩ NTC thermistor on the motor lets the driver stop before the motor overheats. It is optional, and off by default; use it on any motor that runs near its rated current for long.

Figure 11: The thermistor on its 2-pin connector.

docs.title: Fitting it
docs.text:
A stepper is sealed: the windings cannot be reached. Place the thermistor on the motor housing, as close to the windings as possible: either glued to the side of the housing, or in one of the four screw holes of the motor's bottom with the screw removed, which puts it deep in the stack. Thermal cement holds it and conducts the heat.

The housing lags behind the windings by some seconds, and reads lower. Set the limit with that in mind: the default of 75 °C at the housing corresponds to a hotter winding.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
#Term 1
#Tlim 75
#Save

#Temp then prints the temperature; with the thermistor disabled it prints Temp Off. Above the limit the driver raises a temperature error and stops; it clears with #Clear once the motor has cooled.

Over CAN, Send_Respond_Temperature returns the temperature, and the temperature error is one of the bits of Send_Respond_State_of_Errors.

docs.title: Wiring the stepper
docs.text:
A bipolar stepper has two coils and four wires. One coil goes to the terminals A+ and A−, the other to B+ and B−. Which coil is A and which is B does not matter, and neither does the polarity of each coil: firmware 105 and newer finds the wiring during calibration and compensates it.

Figure 7: The motor terminals A+, A−, B+, B− and the other connectors.

docs.title: Finding the two coils
docs.text: With a multimeter on the resistance range, the two wires of one coil show the coil's resistance, a few ohms; two wires of different coils show no connection. Pair the wires that way. Most datasheets also name the pairs (A/C and B/D, or the colours).

docs.title: Soldering
docs.text:
1. Cut the leads to a comfortable length: long enough to reach the pads with the board mounted, short enough not to get into the motor's shaft. If your firmware is older than 105 (see Releases and versions), leave them long enough to swap one pair later.
  2. Tin the leads and solder them to the pads: one coil to A+ and A−, the other to B+ and B−.
  3. Make sure no strand bridges two pads and that nothing touches the motor housing.

Warning

Never connect or disconnect the motor while the driver is powered.

docs.title: Phase order and direction
docs.text:
Calibration spins the motor in open loop and watches the encoder. With firmware 105 and newer, a reversed coil is detected and compensated in software (the firmware applies a reflection of the current frame, which is what a physical swap would do), so the motor calibrates identically with any wiring, and positive commands turn the motor counter-clockwise seen from the magnet side. With firmware 103, a reversed coil fails the open-loop step with Open loop: Failed / Switch motor phases and try again!; swap A+ and A− and calibrate again.

If you want the other direction to be positive, swap the two wires of one coil and calibrate again, or keep the wiring and use negative setpoints.

docs.title: First setup
docs.text:
From a mounted and wired driver to a calibrated, tuned motor. Motor GUI in the browser is the usual tool for it; every step also gives the terminal command, for a terminal or for the console in Motor GUI.

  1. Motor GUI: the browser, the serial adapter, opening the port, what is on the screen.
  2. The serial terminal: the alternative — PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino monitor, and the # commands.
  3. Motor parameters and calibration: the motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs, then the calibration run.
  4. Current limit and loop tuning: the current limit for the motor, and the loop gains if the defaults do not suit it.
  5. Saving the configuration: nothing survives a power cycle until it is saved.

A driver that has been through these pages is ready for Operation. The Quick start is the same path on one page.

docs.title: Motor parameters and calibration
docs.text:
Calibration teaches the driver its motor: it checks the magnet and the supply, takes the motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs from you, computes the current loop gains, spins the motor in open loop to learn the direction of the wiring, finds the angle offset between the encoder and the motor's electrical zero, and measures the motor constants Kt, KV and the flux linkage. It runs once per motor; the result is kept by saving.

The motor turns

Calibration spins the motor in both directions, fast at times. Fix the motor to the bench and take everything off the shaft.

Supply voltage

Calibrate at 24 V. At a lower voltage the KV and Kt come out wrong.

docs.title: 1. Enter the motor parameters
docs.text:
STEPFOC does not measure the resistance and inductance of a stepper (the Spectral Micro does for a BLDC); you enter them from the motor's datasheet, as the values of one coil, and the pole pairs. Calibration fails on a value left at 0, and accepts only 50, 75, 100 or 125 pole pairs.

Motor GUITerminal

In the motor settings enter Pole pairs (50 for a 1.8° motor, 75 for 1.2°, 100 for 0.9°, 125 for 0.72°), Resistance in ohms and Inductance in henries, and apply them.

#PP 50          1.8° stepper: 50; 1.2°: 75; 0.9°: 100; 0.72°: 125
#R 1.1          phase resistance in ohms
#L 0.0026       phase inductance in henries (2.6 mH)
Figure 17: The three values on a typical datasheet, here for the 17HS16-2004S1: 1.8°, 1.1 Ω, 2.6 mH.

The current loop bandwidth (#Cbw, 500 Hz by default) decides the gains calibration computes from R and L; leave it for now, Current limit and loop tuning comes back to it.

docs.title: 2. Run it
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Start the calibration. The driver enters Calibration mode and the GUI shows its log step by step; when it finishes, the phase order and direction, Kt, KV and the flux linkage it found appear in the settings.

#Cal

The LED flashes every 0.5 s while the routine runs, and the driver prints each step as it goes:

----------------
Calibration mode
----------------
Pole pair test: Passed
Magnet test: Passed
Vbus test: Passed
Resistance = 1.100000Ohm
Inductance = 0.002600H
Kp_iq = ...
Ki_iq = ...
Open loop direction: good
Angle offset is: ...
Phase order is good!
KV is: ...
Kt is: ...
Flux linkage is: ...
----------------
Calibration success!
Save config with #Save
Going to idle!
----------------

What the steps are:

Step What happens Fails with Pole pair test the entered pole pairs are one of 50, 75, 100, 125 Pole pair test: Failed and the list of values Magnet test the encoder sees enough field Magnet test: Failed: magnet missing, too far, or axially magnetised Vbus test the supply is within limits Vbus test: Failed Resistance, inductance the entered values are not 0; they are printed back and Kp_iq, Ki_iq computed from them and the bandwidth Resistance test: Failed / Inductance test: Failed, with Please enter your stepper resistance by using #R command Open loop the motor is stepped open loop; the encoder must see it turn. The direction it turned is remembered, so a reversed coil is compensated from here on Open loop: Failed / Switch motor phases and try again!: the encoder saw no rotation Angle offset the motor is driven to find the offset between encoder zero and electrical zero. It spins quickly one way, then the other, for up to two minutes Phase order is wrong! / Switch motor phases and try again!: the commutation check got no response from the motor on two tries. A line Spin-confirm delta: … ticks (need > 8192), Vbus: … mV says how far the motor turned and at what voltage Kt, KV, flux linkage the motor spins fast for a moment and the constants are computed from the back-EMF —

The two 'Switch motor phases' messages

They are left over from firmware 103, which needed the coils wired a particular way. Since firmware 105 the wiring is detected and compensated, so these messages mean the motor did not turn or did not respond: a coil not connected or shorted, a current limit at 0, a supply too weak, or a magnet that slips. Swapping wires does not fix them.

docs.title: 3. Save
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Save. The GUI marks Unsaved changes until you do.

#Save

Without it the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. The driver goes to idle and the LED shows normal operation; the state shows Calibrated and the constants.

docs.title: When to calibrate again
docs.text:
• After changing the motor, the magnet or the wiring.
  • After restoring the defaults.
  • After a firmware update that clears the calibration (a release note says so when it does).

A calibration that reports success but a motor that runs badly afterwards usually means the magnet moved on the shaft between calibration and use: fix the magnet and calibrate again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Message Cause Magnet test: Failed no magnet, magnet too far (more than about 1.5 mm), or an axially magnetised magnet Vbus test: Failed supply off, too low, or the cable the wrong way round (if the driver survived it) Resistance test: Failed, Inductance test: Failed the resistance or the inductance still 0 Open loop: Failed the motor did not turn: a coil open, the open-loop voltage (#Openv) too low for the motor, no supply current Phase order is wrong! see the note above: the motor did not respond to the commutation check; check the wiring, the current limit and the magnet the routine stops in a step and prints nothing more reset the driver (#Reset) and try again success, but the LED stays on and no error is reported the state shows -1 somewhere: the EEPROM is not in the firmware's layout; restore the defaults, enter the parameters, calibrate again

The angle-offset step alone can be repeated with #Calangle.

docs.title: Motor GUI
docs.text:
Motor GUI is the usual way to set up, test and tune a driver: a tool in the browser that connects to one driver over the serial adapter or to a bus of drivers over the CANvas adapter, shows the state, moves the motor, runs the calibration, tunes the loops with live plots, records telemetry and updates the firmware. Nothing is installed. Everything it does, the driver also does from a terminal or from Python — the GUI reads and writes the same settings — so every procedure in this manual shows the GUI first and the terminal command beside it.

Screenshots follow

Motor GUI is being finished; this page describes what it does and will get its pictures when the tool is done.

docs.title: The browser
docs.text: Motor GUI reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access (Web Serial), which Chromium-based browsers have: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera. Firefox and Safari cannot open serial ports.

docs.title: Two ways to connect
docs.text: Adapter Use it for One driver over serial the 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter on the driver's UART connector, 256000 baud the first setup and calibration (calibration runs over UART only), tuning on the bench A bus over CAN the CANvas adapter; it appears as a serial port and speaks slcan every driver on the bus by its node ID: testing a machine, updating firmware on all joints

docs.title: Opening the port
docs.text:
1. Plug in the adapter and power the driver (the adapter does not power it).
  2. Open motorgui.com, choose the connection kind, and Open port. The browser asks which port; pick the adapter's.
  3. The driver's identity appears: hardware version, firmware version, serial number, batch date, whether it is calibrated and activated, and the active errors — what #Info prints in a terminal.

If the port is not offered, the browser is not Chromium-based, or another program holds the port (a terminal left open, PlatformIO's monitor). If the port opens and nothing appears: the driver is unpowered, or TX and RX are crossed on an adapter that is not the Source Robotics one.

docs.title: What is on the screen
docs.text:
• State: the identity above, the control mode the driver is in, the errors, and Clear errors.
  • Jog: Jog position, Jog velocity and Jog current move the motor in the matching control mode; Send setpoint sends a value in the current mode. Live stream while dragging follows a slider as you move it.
  • Plots of position, speed and current, panning and zooming, with the value under the pointer.
  • Settings: the motor parameters (pole pairs, resistance, inductance), the limits (current, velocity, voltage), the loop gains with Apply gains and Apply preset, the CAN node ID, the watchdog, the thermistor. The GUI marks Unsaved changes until you Save to the driver's EEPROM; Default restores the factory values.
  • Calibration: starts #Cal and shows the driver's log step by step; afterwards the phase order and direction, Kt, KV and the flux linkage it found.
  • Telemetry: the stream from the driver, and recordings of it for a test or a bug report.
  • Firmware update: the releases from GitHub, flashed through the bootloader; Scan bootloaders on a bus.
  • Gripper: the gripper controls, for a driver in gripper mode.
  • Console: type any # command by hand; the answer appears below it.
  • Wiring diagrams and Keyboard shortcuts under help.

docs.title: What next
docs.text: Motor parameters and calibration is the first thing to do with a connected driver; Working in Motor GUI covers everyday use: moving the motor, the plots, recordings, several motors on a bus.

docs.title: Saving the configuration
docs.text:
Nothing you set survives a power cycle until you save it.

Motor GUITerminal

Save. The GUI marks Unsaved changes until you do.

#Save

Saving writes the whole configuration to the EEPROM: the motor parameters and the calibration, every gain and limit, the CAN node ID, the heartbeat and watchdog settings, the thermistor and LED settings and the gripper flag. Over CAN, Send_Save_config does the same. Save after calibration, after tuning, and after changing the node ID.

docs.title: The defaults
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Default in the settings.

#Default

Restoring the defaults writes the factory values to the EEPROM and reloads them. It also resets the serial number, the hardware version and the batch date the driver reports, and clears the gripper flag, the heartbeat rate and the watchdog; note what the driver reports before you use it. The defaults are listed in the Defaults reference.

Use it after a firmware update when the driver behaves oddly, or when the state shows nonsense values (a -1 where a number should be): the EEPROM then holds a layout the firmware does not expect.

docs.title: What the driver reports
docs.text: The state Motor GUI shows, and #Info prints, is what is in the EEPROM and what the driver measures: hardware and firmware version, serial number, calibration state, resistance, inductance, pole pairs, Kt and KV, the gains and limits, the CAN ID, and the active errors. It is the first thing to look at when something is off, and the thing to copy into a bug report.

docs.title: The serial terminal
docs.text:
Motor GUI is the usual way to work with the driver; a plain serial terminal is the alternative, and it is what the console inside Motor GUI is. Everything in this manual that is done in the GUI is also one # command, and the terminal shows the driver's answers exactly as it prints them, which is useful when something does not work.

The driver talks on its UART connector at 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V. Any terminal that sends a line ending in CR+LF works.

Figure 12: The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
1. Plug the USB-to-serial adapter into the UART connector with the UART cable. With another adapter: 3.3 V only, and cross TX and RX.
  2. Power the driver. The USB adapter does not power it.
  3. Find the adapter's port: COM… on Windows, /dev/ttyUSB… or /dev/ttyACM… on Linux and macOS.

Danger

5 V on the UART pins destroys the board.

docs.title: A terminal
docs.text:
PuTTYVS Code (PlatformIO)Arduino IDE

PuTTY needs to send CR+LF when you press Enter, which the stock build cannot. Use the modified PuTTY: under Terminal → Keyboard select the CR LF option, then open the serial port at 256000.

Keyboard setting Session

With the firmware project open in VS Code with the PlatformIO extension, the serial monitor (the plug icon in the status bar) uses the speed and the send_on_enter filter from platformio.ini, so a line goes out with CR+LF when you press Enter.

platformio.ini The monitor

Select the adapter's port under Tools, any board (the monitor does not care), open the serial monitor, set 256000 baud and Both NL & CR as the line ending.

docs.title: The first commands
docs.text:
#Info

prints the driver's identity: the hardware and firmware version, the serial number, the motor parameters and the calibration state. #Help (firmware 108) prints a short command reference, #Error the active errors.

Every command starts with #, and a Set/Get command takes one number after a space: #P 16384 moves to position 16384; #P alone prints the position. Names are case-sensitive. The whole set is in the UART commands reference, and Over UART explains the protocol.

docs.title: Current limit and loop tuning
docs.text: Calibration leaves the driver with current loop gains computed for your motor and with conservative velocity and position gains. Two things remain: the current limit, which you must set for your motor, and the loop gains, which you tune if the defaults do not suit it. Motor GUI shows the motor's response on its plots while you change a gain, which is what makes tuning quick.

docs.title: The current limit
docs.text:
Set the current limit to the rated phase current of your motor in mA (the datasheet value; the tested motors' ratings are in Tested motors). The firmware clamps the limit to the driver's 2800 mA and does not trip on phase current by itself; the MOSFET driver's hardware protection only catches a hard fault. A limit above the motor's rating overheats the motor.

Motor GUITerminal

In the limits set the current limit, then Save.

#Ilim 1500
#Save

Crunching and whining sounds at speed usually mean the current limit, or the current loop gains, are too high.

docs.title: The loops
docs.text:
Figure 13: The position loop commands the velocity loop, which commands the current loop.

Tune from the inside out: the current loop first, then velocity, then position. Before you start:

  • The motor must be calibrated and without active errors; the driver refuses the control modes otherwise.
  • Fix the motor to the bench, nothing on the shaft. A loop that oscillates can shake a loose motor off the table.
  • If the defaults oscillate, lower all gains until the motor is quiet, then raise them one at a time in small steps.
Motor GUITerminal

The gains are in the settings: change one, Apply gains, command a move with the jog controls and read the response on the plots. Apply preset loads a starting set for a kind of motor. Save when you are done.

Each gain is a command: #Kpiq 0.5, #Kpv 0.02, …, then #Save. Command a move with #Iq, #V or #P and judge the response by ear and by #Cyc 20, which streams position, speed and current.

docs.title: The current loop
docs.text:
The current loop is a PI controller that turns a current request into a voltage. Calibration sets its gains Kpiq and Kiiq from the motor's resistance and inductance and the bandwidth (#Cbw, 500 Hz by default; set it before calibrating). For a stepper these computed gains are a starting point; tune by hand if the motor hums or responds slowly:

  1. Raise Kpiq until the motor starts to hum or oscillate, then back off 20 %.
  2. Raise Kiiq the same way, then back off a little.
  3. Test with a current setpoint of a few hundred mA (Jog current, or #Iq 300): the motor should push with a steady, quiet torque. Keep the current well under the limit.

A higher bandwidth responds faster to a disturbance and is louder; 800 Hz and more is common in industry, and useful for legged robots.

docs.title: The velocity loop
docs.text:
1. Raise Kpv until the motor oscillates at a steady speed command, then back off 20 %.
  2. Raise Kiv slowly until it oscillates, then back off a little. Kiv is an integrator: too much makes the motor unstable, none leaves a steady-state error.
  3. Test with a speed setpoint (Jog velocity, or #V 20000; 16384 ticks per second is one revolution per second) and with different speeds.

docs.title: The position loop
docs.text:
1. Raise Kpp until the motor overshoots or oscillates when it reaches a target, then back off.
  2. Test with a position step (Jog position, or #P 16384 and #P 0): one revolution and back. The response should be quick, without overshoot; the plot shows both.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Run the motor over the whole range of speeds and loads it will see, with a load if you can, and adjust. Then save.

docs.title: Impedance (PD) mode
docs.text:
Figure 14: The impedance loop: a spring (KP) and a damper (KD) around the position setpoint, plus a current feedforward.

In PD mode the motor behaves like a spring and a damper: the torque is KP × (setpoint − position) + KD × (speed setpoint − speed) + feedforward current. Set KP and KD (the gains, or #KP, #KD, or Send_PD_Gains), then command with #PD, #PDV and #PDI or Send_data_pack_PD. Start with a small KP and KD of 0, raise KP until the motor holds position firmly, then add KD until it stops ringing. The theory corner explains the loop.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The velocity limit (#Vlimit) clamps the speed the loops may command, in encoder ticks per second. A rough maximum for your motor is 0.8 × Vbus × KV × 16384 / 60 ticks per second, with KV from calibration.
  • The voltage limit (#Vlim) clamps the voltage of the current loops in mV; 0 uses the supply voltage.
  • #Rstint 1 resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which avoids windup when a program sends one setpoint after another with large steps.

docs.title: Operation
docs.text: How a calibrated driver is used: the control modes and what each one does, the two ways to talk to the driver and the two tools on top of them, what happens when something goes wrong, and gripper mode.

docs.title: In this chapter
